title: Prescriptive benchmarks for mixed workloads (draft)
body:
Purpose:

Quick prescriptive benchmark notes and recommended starter presets for mixed inference workloads (chat + short completions + embeddings + reranking). This is a working draft — goal is a set of minimal, safe presets we can push as defaults in the Optimize UI and a short A/B plan to validate quality vs cost.

Context / motivation:
- Customers run 2–3 modes in the same route: interactive chat (low tail latency), bulk short completions (throughput optimized), and occasional embedding/rerank calls.
- Current default presets bias toward throughput; we need a small family of recommended profiles that balance latency SLOs and unit cost for mixed traffic.
- There are existing spreadsheets (linked) with full simulation inputs; this doc summarizes recommended starting points and runbook for experiments.

High-level constraints we used for these presets:
- Chat SLOs: median < 80ms CPU-side decode, p95 < 250ms.
- Completion SLOs (bulk): prioritize throughput, target token/sec per GPU > baseline.
- Embeddings: batch aggressively up to 256 or 512 items where possible.
- Quality guardrail: no more than 2% measured drop in evaluator prompt sets per rollout step.

Definitions / names used below (simple):
- preset: a named bundle of batching + cache + quant settings we can attach to a route.
- sample_latency_target_ms: target request-level latency we tune batching for.
- kv_cache_ttl_s: how long prefix/KV entries are kept in memory for reuse.
- quant_profile: recommended quantization type to serve (e.g., INT8, NF4-like, AWQ-4).

Recommended starter presets (short descriptions + numeric starters):

1) preset: mixed-low-latency (chat-first)
- intended for: interactive chat apps with occasional completions
- max_batch_size: 8
- adaptive_batch_target_ms: 25
- max_batch_delay_ms: 15
- kv_cache_policy: prefix-heavy (cache prefixes aggressively)
- kv_cache_ttl_s: 60
- quant_profile: int8-first (serve INT8 by default, keep fp16 variant as fallback)
- expected cost delta vs current baseline: -12% to -20% (simulated)
- quality guardrail: run evaluator set A, require <1.5% regression

Rationale: keep batch sizes small so per-request tail latency remains low while still getting some batching benefits. Longer prefix TTL helps for multi-turn chat. INT8 preserves most quality while reducing GPU memory and throughput cost.

2) preset: throughput-cost (bulk short-comps)
- intended for: high-rate short completions, low quality sensitivity
- max_batch_size: 64
- adaptive_batch_target_ms: 120
- max_batch_delay_ms: 60
- kv_cache_policy: opportunistic (cache only if prefix reused > 10% historically)
- kv_cache_ttl_s: 6
- quant_profile: aggressive-4bit (test NF4/AWQ-4) with fp16 fallback
- expected cost delta vs baseline: -30% to -45% (simulated wide range depending on payloads)
- quality guardrail: require A/B test to show acceptable degradation on sample prompts (allow up to 3% for low-sensitivity workloads)

Rationale: big batches amortize decoding cost; aggressive quantization yields the most savings. Keep short TTL to avoid memory pressure when working sets are large.

3) preset: embeddings-high-batch
- intended for: embeddings pipelines, offline/nearline transforms
- max_batch_size: 512
- adaptive_batch_target_ms: 500
- max_batch_delay_ms: 200
- kv_cache_policy: none (embeddings typically stateless)
- kv_cache_ttl_s: 0
- quant_profile: int8 or mixed-precision (embedding model specific)
- expected cost delta vs baseline: -20% to -40%

Rationale: embeddings are cheap to batch aggressively; kernel selection should focus on throughput kernels. Cache is not useful for stateless inputs.

4) preset: rerank-latency-balanced
- intended for: reranking tasks called synchronously within user flows
- max_batch_size: 16
- adaptive_batch_target_ms: 60
- max_batch_delay_ms: 30
- kv_cache_policy: small-window (cache very recent prefixes for 10-20s)
- kv_cache_ttl_s: 15
- quant_profile: int8 with per-route fallback to fp16 for sensitive models
- expected cost delta: -10% to -25%

Rationale: keep latency tight but allow some batching for short ranking lists. Prefer conservative quant to avoid subtle score shifts.

Quantization guidance (experiments to run):
- Phase 0: baseline measure in spreadsheet with fp16 across workloads (single run). Capture token/sec, tail latencies, mem usage.
- Phase 1: INT8 rollouts: enable int8 for mixed-low-latency and embeddings-high-batch routes. Run evaluator suites and live canary (1% traffic).
- Phase 2: NF4/AWQ-4 for throughput-cost preset only. Validate with offline prompt sets and a focused human review for high-impact prompts.
- Rollback: automatic fallback to fp16 on quality regression or latency anomalies.

Caching notes:
- Prefix/KV caching helps chat and rerank; TTL should reflect typical conversation cadence. We used 60s for chat-first as a starting point.
- For routes with many unique prefixes (search queries, few repeats), keep TTL < 10s to avoid wasted memory.
- Implement cache pressure evictions by LRU and track cache hit rate metric (target > 25% for caching to be worth memory).

Spreadsheet model assumptions (summary):
- GPU model: A100-like baseline, with kernels optimized for INT8 and NF4.
- Average token lengths: chat request 12 tokens input + 48 tokens output; completion short 6 in + 12 out; embedding payload 512 chars => 2 tokens per item (effective batch optimized).
- Price model: dollars per GPU-hour mapped to per-token cost in linked sheet.
- Simulated traffic mixes: 60% chat, 30% completions, 10% embeddings; alternate mixes in separate tabs.

Expected outcomes and TL;DR:
- Reasonable defaults (the 4 presets above) cover most mixed traffic scenarios and should reduce unit cost 10–40% depending on workload composition.
- Conservative quantization (INT8) is the lowest-risk win; more aggressive 4-bit profiles bring larger savings but require focused QA.
- A small canary + evaluator-runbook is mandatory before any broad rollout.

Runbook for rolling these presets (short):
1) Create presets in an internal feature-flagged UI (dev-only first).
2) Run synthetic loads using the spreadsheet batch inputs (reproduce baseline metrics).
3) Canary to 1% live traffic for each preset group for 48 hours; collect detailed token-level metrics + evaluator results.
4) If regressions within guardrail, rollback preset for that route and schedule targeted quality tuning (adjust quant profile or increase batch conservative thresholds).
5) If green, expand to 10% for another 48–72 hours, then 50%, then 100% with close monitoring.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need a short evaluator set specifically for reranking score sensitivity (Devon to draft).
- Instrumentation: add per-route quant_profile metric and per-request chosen_kernel tag (Mateo).
- Memory pressure thresholds: define safe kv_cache_ttl heuristics per-node (SRE + infra).
- Spreadsheet: add Monte Carlo runs for workload mix uncertainty (Rina).

Notes to reviewer:
- This is intentionally prescriptive and conservative in the chat/rerank contexts. Feel free to suggest different numeric starters — we want a small set of easy-to-expose presets that reduce friction for customers and internal teams.

References and links (inlined):
- cost sims sheet: https://drive.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1costsim-mixed-2024
- canary checklist: Confluence/optimize/canary-runbook (placeholder)
